title: Do Quebec police recruits get enough racial profiling training? We checked the curriculum
summary: At Quebec's provincial police academy, aspiring officers spend hundreds of hours on technical skills crucial to the job, from firing weapons to physically restraining suspects. Far less of their time…

image.caption: The École nationale de police du Québec in Nicolet, Que., where aspiring officers must complete a 15-week training program before joining a Quebec police force. (Olivier Croteau/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

At Quebec's provincial police academy, aspiring officers spend hundreds of hours on technical skills crucial to the job, from firing weapons to physically restraining suspects. Far less of their time explicitly addresses issues such as racial profiling and ethical breaches — which led to the firing of seven Montreal police officers earlier this month.
Documents detail what aspiring officers learn at province's police academy
Before becoming a police officer in Quebec, recruits must first complete a 15-week course at the provincial police academy.
There, they spend hundreds of hours on technical skills crucial to the job, from firing weapons to physically restraining suspects.
Far less of their time explicitly addresses issues such as racial profiling and ethical breaches — which led to the firing of seven Montreal police officers earlier this month.

According to curriculum documents obtained by CBC News under access-to-information legislation, 11.5 hours of course work is dedicated to "diversity and racial profiling" and a little over three hours to "Indigenous realities."
By comparison, 31.5 hours is allotted to driving a police vehicle, for example, and 14.5 hours is set aside for securing a perimeter after arriving first at a scene.

While the École nationale de police du Québec (ENPQ) maintains that themes such as diversity training and ethics are woven through its 377-hour program, critics say the lack of emphasis sends the wrong message to aspiring officers.

"The training is mostly based on use of force and not enough on how to interact and take into consideration the issues of human rights, racial profiling and Indigenous relations," said Lynda Khelil, a spokesperson for the civil rights advocacy group Ligue des droits et libertés.
What's in the program?

The ENPQ documents lay out in detail the academy's program, which must be completed before a police officer can work in Quebec. The program is intended to build on the three-year police program at the CEGEP level, and prepare them for the daily realities of policing.
It is also meant to ensure that police officers "safeguard rights and freedoms, respect victims and co-operate with the community while respecting cultural pluralism."
The ENPQ did not provide details about its racial profiling training as part of the access-to-information request, saying it could not share teaching material used to evaluate students.

Paul Chablo, chairperson of the police technology program at John Abbott College, said CEGEPs carry much of the weight when it comes to teaching the sociology and ethics of the job, including the difference between criminal and racial profiling.
In his view, the recent firing of the seven SPVM officers shows that college-level ethics training is taking root, since fellow officers reported the misconduct.
"That was unheard of 30 years ago," said Chablo, a former SPVM officer.
Police academy tries to recreate real environment

Véronique Brunet, a spokesperson for the ENPQ, said the training for aspiring officers strikes the right balance, and that the hourly breakdown of coursework doesn't reflect the full range of what students learn.
Issues such as racial profiling or dealing with diverse communities are built into many of the scenarios during the training, she said.
"We try to recreate the real environment as much as possible," she said, noting that 80 per cent of the training is practical.

blocks.text: She added, as well, that the curriculum is continuously being updated.

"Everything happening in society — whether generally, or through a coroner's report, an investigation, or a ministerial directive — will shape program development, and the program adjusts continuously."
At the CEGEP level, between 45 and 105 hours are devoted to "Indigenous realities and ethnocultural communities," she said.
Still, the training for police has come under scrutiny in recent months, with Montreal police in the spotlight for a series of scandals.

Earlier this month, Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher announced the firing of seven officers in connection with allegations of discriminatory and racist behaviour.
The specific reasons for their dismissals haven't been made public.

Over the past few months, allegations against officers across two stations include targeting Black and Arab people and collecting their hair as trophies; committing discriminatory acts toward homeless people; and deleting video evidence from an alleged victim's phone related to an intimate partner violence investigation.
Influx of new officers
Montreal police, also known as the SPVM, has hired more than 1,000 officers over the past three years.

Dagher has said many of the officers involved in the alleged wrongdoing had less than five years' experience with the police. He said changes are forthcoming to the SPVM's approach to recruitment and training.

blocks.text: The SPVM would not comment on the ENPQ's program, but noted that all new officers must already complete an eight-week police integration program of its own.
For five of those weeks, recruits are stripped of their weapons and uniforms and sent to work alongside community organizations in a program called "Immersion MTL."

The goal, according to the SPVM, is to build trust among the population.

Recruits participate in activities such as distributing food, assisting people with mental health or neurodevelopmental challenges, joining French classes for newcomers and meeting with people who have recently been incarcerated.
Massimiliano Mulone, an associate professor of criminology at Université de Montréal, argued that more training isn't necessarily going to solve the problem of racial profiling.

blocks.text: He said Montreal police need to change the structure of police work, starting with street checks, which have been widely criticized for disproportionately targeting minorities.
"I don't think that the fault should be put on the police officers. I think that the fault should be put on the police organization. We have to change the police, not the police officers."
